Native defaults in 0.15.0

Source: vignettes/articles/native-defaults-0-15.qmd

medfit 0.15.0 changed two defaults of fit_sem() and fit_mediation(engine = "native"), so that a default native fit is posed like a default lavaan fit with fixed.x = TRUE and meanstructure = TRUE:

Argument Default through 0.14.x Default from 0.15.0 lavaan equivalent
fixed_x FALSE (every exogenous moment is a parameter) the observed exogenous variables fixed.x = TRUE
meanstructure NULL (means only when the syntax writes ~1 or a product) TRUE meanstructure = TRUE

This page explains both changes with the same depth: what each one does to the likelihood, why the structural estimates and their standard errors stay put, which reported numbers move, and how the change was checked. Every formula is in Methods and Formulas; the derivations are in the native mini-book, chapter 1 (the mean structure) and chapter 4 (fixed exogenous variables).

What changed and when

  • 0.14.0 changed no result. A native fit that left fixed_x or meanstructure unset, in a model where that default would matter, warned once per session per argument (class medfit_warning_default_change).
  • 0.15.0 flips both defaults together, after the notice in issue #329. The 0.14.0 warning no longer fires. FALSE and NULL stay valid values in every release, and an explicit argument is always kept as given.
  • 0.16.0 removes options(medfit.native_defaults). Since 0.15.0 the option is ignored; setting it gives one message per session (class medfit_message_option_obsolete) and changes nothing.

Two ways to act:

  1. Take the new defaults. Leave both arguments unset. Expect the changes listed below: the conditional logLik(), the parameter count, AIC and BIC, and the names in coef(), vcov() and tidy().
  2. Keep the 0.14.x results. Pass both arguments: fit_sem(model, data, fixed_x = FALSE, meanstructure = NULL). The results are those of 0.14.x. Package authors who need identical results across releases pass both arguments in code, examples and tests.

A recipe for packages that depend on medfit

A package that must give the 0.14.x results with medfit releases before and after 0.14.0 cannot pass meanstructure to a medfit that lacks it. Check the formals first, then pass the arguments the installed medfit knows and the caller left unset:

.fit_sem <- function(...) {
  args <- list(...)
  f <- names(formals(medfit::fit_sem))
  if ("fixed_x" %in% f && !"fixed_x" %in% names(args)) args$fixed_x <- FALSE
  if ("meanstructure" %in% f && !"meanstructure" %in% names(args)) {
    args["meanstructure"] <- list(NULL)
  }
  do.call(medfit::fit_sem, args)
}

args["meanstructure"] <- list(NULL) stores an explicit NULL; args$meanstructure <- NULL would delete the element and leave the default in force, which since 0.15.0 means the mean structure is on and the wrapper’s intended covariance-only fit is silently lost. RMediation’s test helper uses this wrapper (Data-Wise/rmediation#85).

The worked example

One mediator, one covariate, so two exogenous observed variables (treatment and covariate1) and \(p = 4\) observed variables in all.

library(medfit)

Attaching package: 'medfit'
The following object is masked from 'package:stats':

    decompose
library(generics)

Attaching package: 'generics'
The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    as.difftime, as.factor, as.ordered, intersect, is.element, setdiff,
    setequal, union
model <- "
  mediator1 ~ a * treatment + covariate1
  outcome ~ b * mediator1 + cp * treatment + covariate1
"

Each combination of the two arguments is set explicitly:

settings <- expand.grid(fixed_x = c(FALSE, TRUE), meanstructure = c(FALSE, TRUE))
rows <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(settings)), function(i) {
  f <- fit_sem(model, mediation_demo,
               fixed_x = settings$fixed_x[i], meanstructure = settings$meanstructure[i])
  ll <- logLik(f)
  se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(f)))
  data.frame(
    fixed_x = settings$fixed_x[i], meanstructure = settings$meanstructure[i],
    npar = length(coef(f)), logLik_df = attr(ll, "df"), logLik = round(as.numeric(ll), 3),
    AIC = round(AIC(f), 3),
    a = round(coef(f)[["a"]], 6), b = round(coef(f)[["b"]], 6), cp = round(coef(f)[["cp"]], 6),
    se_a = round(se[["a"]], 6), se_b = round(se[["b"]], 6), se_cp = round(se[["cp"]], 6)
  )
})
four <- do.call(rbind, rows)
four
  fixed_x meanstructure npar logLik_df    logLik      AIC        a        b
1   FALSE         FALSE   10        14 -2001.826 4031.651 0.581425 0.572944
2    TRUE         FALSE    7         9 -1139.928 2297.856 0.581425 0.572944
3   FALSE          TRUE   14        14 -2001.826 4031.651 0.581425 0.572944
4    TRUE          TRUE    9         9 -1139.928 2297.856 0.581425 0.572944
       cp     se_a     se_b    se_cp
1 0.20426 0.098585 0.053065 0.109082
2 0.20426 0.098585 0.053065 0.109082
3 0.20426 0.098585 0.053065 0.109082
4 0.20426 0.098585 0.053065 0.109082

Read the table by column:

  • a, b, cp and their standard errors are identical in all four rows.
  • fixed_x = TRUE drops three parameters without a mean structure (the two exogenous variances and their covariance) and five with one (the same three plus the two exogenous means). logLik and AIC change because the likelihood becomes conditional.
  • meanstructure = TRUE adds one intercept for each observed variable whose mean is not fixed: four with fixed_x = FALSE, two with fixed_x = TRUE. logLik and AIC do not change in medfit; the section on AIC and BIC below says where lavaan’s differ.

fixed_x: the conditional likelihood

With fixed_x, the means, variances and covariances of the selected exogenous variables are no longer parameters. They are held at their sample values, with divisor \(n\) (the maximum-likelihood moments, not the \(n - 1\) ones; the conditional likelihood is in Methods and Formulas, fixed exogenous moments). The joint density of the observed variables factors into the marginal density of the exogenous block and the conditional density of the rest given that block; the structural parameters (paths, residual variances, the intercepts of endogenous variables) appear only in the conditional factor. Maximizing the joint likelihood with the exogenous moments free gives those moments their sample values anyway, so fixing them changes neither the structural estimates nor their standard errors. What changes:

  • logLik() is the conditional log likelihood, comparable only across fits with the same fixed set on the same data.
  • The parameter count drops by the number of fixed moments, and AIC() and BIC() with it.
  • The fixed moments leave coef(), vcov() and the free rows of tidy(); tidy() flags them with fixed_x = TRUE.
  • The model chi-square and its degrees of freedom do not change: the fixed moments are removed from both the parameters and the moments being fit.

The 0.15.0 default is a lenient subset

An explicit fixed_x = TRUE errors when the model writes a ~~ or ~1 statement on an exogenous variable, because such a statement asks to estimate a moment that fixed_x would fix. The 0.15.0 default is lenient instead: it fixes every observed exogenous column except those a ~~ or ~1 statement names, and it says which it left free in a message of class medfit_message_fixed_x_lenient (field variables). glance()$fixed_x lists the set that was fixed.

lenient <- fit_sem(paste(model, "covariate1 ~~ covariate1", sep = "\n"), mediation_demo)
fit_sem(): the `fixed_x` default leaves covariate1 free, because the model writes a `~~` or `~1` statement on it; the other exogenous observed variables are fixed. Pass `fixed_x` explicitly to choose.
glance(lenient)$fixed_x
[1] "treatment"

The pairing rule matters here. medfit, like lavaan, adds the covariances among exogenous variables automatically, but an exogenous variable that the model names in a ~~ statement is not paired with the others. In the fit above covariate1 is named, so the covariance between treatment and covariate1 is not in the model: it is 0 unless you write it. That is a modeling choice the syntax makes, not a side effect of fixed_x; the same model in lavaan has the same zero.

Product columns (x:m) and the 0/1 columns of a factor covariate are observed exogenous columns too, so the default fixes them along with the others. lavaan treats them the same way (the oracle matrix below checks it).

meanstructure = TRUE: a saturated mean part

With meanstructure = TRUE every observed variable gets a free intercept (for an exogenous variable, its mean), and the mean part of the model is saturated unless the syntax restricts it (y ~ 0*1). Through 0.14.x the mean structure was on only when the syntax wrote a ~1 row or a product term; the default now turns it on for every model.

Why nothing structural moves: the maximum-likelihood discrepancy is the covariance-only discrepancy plus an additive mean term, a quadratic form in \(\bar x - \mu(\theta)\) (the formula is in Methods and Formulas, mean structure). When the intercepts are free and not shared, the mean term is minimized at zero by \(\hat\mu = \bar x\) for any covariance parameters, so the covariance parameters solve the same problem as without a mean structure, and the information has no cross block between the two parts. The estimates and standard errors of the paths and variances are therefore the same, and the intercepts are the sample means (for an endogenous variable, the intercept that reproduces its sample mean).

What moves:

  • The parameter vector gains the intercepts: coef(), vcov() and tidy() have new rows.
  • The parameter count rises by the number of free intercepts, so glance()$npar changes.
  • logLik() contains the mean term. For a saturated mean part that term is zero at the solution, so the value is the same as the covariance-only fit’s; medfit already counts the implicit means in the covariance-only fit’s logLik() degrees of freedom (next section), so AIC() and BIC() are the same in medfit too. In the worked example the logLik_df column shows it.
  • Weighted fits: glance() reports NA for chi-square, logLik, AIC and BIC of a fit with weights, with or without a mean structure, because the weighted discrepancy is not a likelihood.

AIC and BIC against lavaan

AIC() and BIC() keep medfit’s own parameter count: the logLik() degrees of freedom are the free parameters plus the observed means that are not fixed, whether or not those means are in the parameter vector (without a mean structure they are, implicitly, at the sample means). That count equals lavaan’s npar when lavaan fits the mean structure, so medfit’s AIC and BIC equal lavaan’s with meanstructure = TRUE, under any fixed_x. A default lavaan::sem() fits no mean structure and counts only its own parameters, so against that fit medfit’s AIC is larger by \(2k\) and its BIC by \(k \log n\), where \(k\) is the number of observed means that are not fixed. The log likelihoods agree in both comparisons. The 0.15.0 default fixes the exogenous variables, so in the worked example \(k = 2\) (the two endogenous variables), and the gap is 4:

default_fit <- fit_sem(model, mediation_demo)
lv_default <- lavaan::sem(model, mediation_demo)
lv_means <- lavaan::sem(model, mediation_demo, meanstructure = TRUE)
c(lavaan_default = lavaan::fitMeasures(lv_default, "aic")[[1]],
  lavaan_means = lavaan::fitMeasures(lv_means, "aic")[[1]],
  medfit = AIC(default_fit))
lavaan_default   lavaan_means         medfit
      2293.856       2297.856       2297.856

Compare AIC and BIC across engines only with the same mean structure on both sides; within medfit the count is the same under every setting, so comparisons between medfit fits are unaffected.

Missing data

The native engine drops incomplete rows (listwise deletion) before it fits, and fixed_x moments are the sample moments of those rows. There is no missing = argument and no full-information maximum likelihood; lavaan’s missing = "fiml" has no counterpart yet.

Evidence: the oracle matrix

tests/sim/native-defaults-oracle.R fits a set of model cells (simple mediation, latent mediator, named and lenient subsets, sampling weights, a four-way product term, a factor covariate) under every combination of the two arguments (and the retired opt-in), and compares structural estimates, standard errors, chi-square, df, logLik, the parameter count, AIC and BIC with lavaan or a stated oracle. It has 557 rows: 503 agree, 54 are recorded limits, 0 block. Each limit is a difference of reporting, declared with its reason, never a widened tolerance:

  • Weights: glance() reports NA for chi-square, logLik, AIC and BIC by design; lavaan reports its weighted-ML values.
  • Covariance-only AIC and BIC: the \(2k\) and \(k \log n\) gap above, in the simple, latent, subset and factor cells under meanstructure = NULL, where the reference lavaan fit has no mean structure. It disappears when lavaan is fitted with meanstructure = TRUE.
  • Product terms: a product turns medfit’s mean structure on while lavaan’s default fits no means, so under meanstructure = NULL the parameter count, AIC and BIC differ by the free means (logLik, estimates and standard errors agree). When a product factor is a regression target, medfit reports chi-square and df as NA because the model test is invalid there; lavaan reports numbers for the same model.

No row disagrees on a structural estimate or its standard error. The retry seed of a multi-start fit is derived from the parameter names, so the larger or smaller parameter vector changes the random starts; a well-identified fit gives the same estimates, but which start wins, and whether the start-spread warning appears, can change.

compare_lr() under the new defaults

compare_lr() accepts fits made under the 0.15.0 defaults (a saturated mean structure and fixed_x), in lavaan and in OpenMx. Its known limit does not change with the flip: a general-purpose optimizer handed the product null can stop above medfit’s reference, and compare_lr() reports that as a classed warning rather than blaming either side. On the pinned design (15 seeds by 4 cells) lavaan ended above the reference in 18 of 60 runs and OpenMx in 13 of 60, the same counts as under 0.14.x, with no mislabeled row (issue #320).
